questions.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of two rows of three. Display the grid itself, in the form [[9, 4, 1], [7, 0, 2]].

teach.say: A two-dimensional list is a list whose items are themselves lists. Build each row as its own list, then append that row to the grid.

brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The last three fill row 1.
Print the grid itself, both sets of brackets and all.
questions.starter: # Two rows of three, then print the grid

tests.why: Two sets of square brackets inside one. A single [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] is one flat list instead of a list of lists.
The numbers fill the first row before the second: reading them down the columns would give [[9, 7, 5], [8, 6, 4]].
Build a fresh inner list for each row - reusing the same one leaves both rows pointing at the same three numbers.

questions.fb: Make an empty row list, append three numbers to it, then append that row to the grid - and start a new row list for the next row.

questions.q: Ask the user for six words, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of two. Display the grid itself, in the form [['red', 'blue'], ['green', 'teal'], ['grey', 'pink']].
brief: The first two words typed fill row 0.
The next two fill row 1.
The last two fill row 2.
Print the grid itself, both sets of brackets and the quote marks and all.
questions.starter: # Three rows of two words, then print the grid

tests.why: Three inner lists of two words each, filled a row at a time.
Build a fresh inner list for each row - reusing the same one leaves every row holding the same two words.
Three rows of two, not two rows of three, so the shape comes from the two range() numbers.

questions.fb: The two range() numbers decide the shape: the outer one counts the rows and the inner one counts the items in each row.

questions.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a row number, counting from 0. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of two. Display [that whole row as a list], square brackets and all.
brief: The first two numbers typed fill row 0.
The row number is always one the grid has.
questions.starter: # Three rows of two, then print one whole row

tests.why: Row 1 is the second row, because the counting starts at 0.
Row 0 is the first row. Printing [2, 7] means the rows were counted from 1.
Three rows means 2 is the last row number, and adding 1 would run off the end of the grid.
A different grid, so a row typed in by hand fails here. Printing grid[r] gives the brackets and commas for you.

questions.fb: grid[r] is one whole row of the grid, and printing it shows the brackets and commas for you.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a row number. Then ask for a column number. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of three. Display [the value stored there] and nothing else.

teach.say: Two sets of brackets: the first picks a row out of the grid, the second picks an item out of that row.

brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Both the row and the column count from 0.
Both numbers are always ones the grid has.
questions.starter: # Three rows of three, then one value out of it

tests.why: The row comes first and the column second, so grid[2][1] would give 3 instead.
Row 0, column 0 is the very first value. Printing 8 means grid[1][1] was used, so both numbers were counted from 1.
Here the two numbers are the other way round from the first test, so a program that reads the column first fails.
Three rows of three means the last value is at [2][2], and [3][3] is past the end of the grid.
A different grid, so a value typed in by hand fails here.

questions.fb: grid[r] is a whole row and grid[r][c] is one item of that row, so the row number always comes first.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a row number, counting from 0. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of three. Display [that whole row] on one line.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Put single spaces between the values.
Print no brackets and no commas.
questions.starter: # Print one whole row across the screen

tests.why: Row 1 is the second row, printed across one line rather than down three.
Row 0 is the first row. Printing 5 2 9 means the rows were counted from 1.
Three rows means 2 is the last row number, and counting from 1 would crash here.
A different grid. Brackets or commas in the output mean the row was printed as a list instead of being built into a line.

questions.fb: A row is one item of the grid, so build its values into a single line and print that line once.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a column number, counting from 0. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of three. Display [that whole column] on one line.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The values go in order from the top row down.
Put single spaces between the values.
Print no brackets and no commas.
questions.starter: # Print one whole column across the screen

tests.why: A column is not stored anywhere, so it has to be gathered by taking grid[i][c] from every row in turn.
Column 0 runs down the left-hand side. Printing 3 6 1 means row 0 was printed instead of column 0.
Three columns means 2 is the last column number, and counting from 1 would crash here.
A different grid, so a column typed in by hand fails here.

questions.fb: A column is not stored anywhere, so you collect it one row at a time with the column number held still.

questions.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of two rows of three. Display each row on its own line.

teach.say: A loop over a grid hands you one row at a time, and a loop inside it walks along that row.

brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Row 0 is printed first.
Two lines of output.
Put single spaces between the values.
Print no brackets and no commas.
questions.starter: # Two rows in, two tidy lines out

tests.why: Two lines of three. Printing the grid itself would give the brackets and commas the question rules out.
The rows stay separate even when the values repeat - a single print inside both loops would give six lines instead of two.
Build the whole line first and print it once, or use print(v, end=' ') and then an empty print at the end of each row.

questions.fb: The outer loop is the rows and the inner loop is the values in one row, so the line break belongs to the outer loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of three. Display one line for every value, in the form [row] [column] [value].
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Rows and columns count from 0.
All of row 0 is printed first.
Nine lines of output.
Put single spaces between the three numbers on a line.
questions.starter: # Visit every value and say where it is

tests.why: The first line must be 0 0 1. If it says 1 1 1 both counts started at 1 instead of 0.
With every value the same only the positions change, which shows plainly that they run 0 to 2 in both directions.
Nine lines in all. Six or three means one of the loops is not running the full three times, or the print is in the wrong loop.

questions.fb: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop counts the columns, so the inner one finishes once for every single step of the outer one.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of three. Display every value that is 10 or more, one on each line. Display none instead, on a line of its own, when there are no such values.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Row 0 is searched first.
Exactly 10 counts as 10 or more.
Print exactly: none
questions.starter: # Pick out the large values, wherever they are in the grid

tests.why: Three values reach 10, and they come out in the order the grid is walked: row 0 first, then row 1, then row 2.
Nothing reaches 10, so the one word is printed. An empty output means the none case was never checked.
Exactly 10 counts, so it is printed. Nothing here means > 10 was used instead of >= 10.
The only large value is the very last one, so a search that stops before the end of the last row never finds it.

questions.fb: Walking every cell with two loops and testing each value is the shape of every search through a grid.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a row number, counting from 0. Store the numbers in a grid of three rows of four. Add up that row. Display [the total] and nothing else.

teach.say: grid[r] is one whole row, and a row is an ordinary list, so you can total it the way you would total any list.

brief: The first four numbers typed fill row 0.
The row number is always one the grid has.
questions.starter: # Three rows of four, then the total of one row

tests.why: Row 1 is 4, 4, 0, 7 which comes to 15. Totalling the first value of every row would give 6 whichever row was asked for.
Row 0 is 2, 5, 3, 1 which comes to 11. An answer of 15 is row 1, so the rows were counted from 1.
Zeros add nothing but the loop still has to visit them, so 0, 0, 9, 3 comes to 12.
A row of zeros still has a total, and it still has to be printed.

questions.fb: grid[r] is a single row and behaves like any other list, so a running total over it works exactly as it always did.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of four. Add up each row in turn. Display [the total of each row], one on each line.
brief: The first four numbers typed fill row 0.
The total of row 0 is printed first.
Three lines of output.
questions.starter: # A total for each row in turn

tests.why: Three row totals, one on each line, in the order the rows were filled.
A row of zeros still prints its total of 0 and must not be skipped.
If every line is the same, the row total was never set back to 0 at the start of each row.

questions.fb: Set the row total back to 0 at the top of the outer loop, so each row's answer is its own.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of three rows of four. Add up each row in turn. Add up the whole grid as well. Display [the total of each row], one on each line. Then display [the total of the whole grid] on the last line.
brief: The first four numbers typed fill row 0.
The total of row 0 is printed first.
Four lines of output in all.
questions.starter: # A total for each row, then one for everything

tests.why: Three row totals and then the grand total, so four lines in all - leaving the last line out loses a mark even when the rows are right.
A row of zeros still prints its total of 0, and the grand total still includes it.
If every row total is the same as the grand total, the row total was never set back to 0 at the start of each row.

questions.fb: Set the row total to 0 inside the outer loop and keep a separate grand total outside it that never gets reset.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a column number, counting from 0. Store the numbers in a grid of four rows of three. Add up that column. Display [the total] and nothing else.

teach.say: A column is not stored anywhere, so you gather it one row at a time: the column number stays still while the row number changes.

brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The column number is always one the grid has.
questions.starter: # Four rows of three, then the total of one column

tests.why: Column 1 is 7, 1, 6, 2 which comes to 16, gathered with grid[r][c] from every row in turn.
Column 0 is 3, 5, 0, 9 which comes to 17. An answer of 12 means row 0 was totalled instead.
Three columns means 2 is the last one, and counting from 1 would ask for column 3 and crash.
Every value in column 1 is 0, so the total is 0. A 4 here means column 0 was totalled whatever was asked for.

questions.fb: Loop over the rows with range(len(grid)) and hold the column number still - that is the one difference from totalling a row.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of four rows of three. Add up each column in turn. Display [the total of each column], one on each line.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The total of column 0 is printed first.
Three lines of output.
questions.starter: # A total for each column in turn

tests.why: Three column totals, one on each line. Getting 6, 15, 24 and 33 means the rows were totalled instead.
Only column 0 has anything in it, and the other two still print a total of 0 rather than being skipped.
Here it is the last column that holds everything, so a loop that stops one column short would print only two lines.

questions.fb: For column totals the outer loop counts columns and the inner loop counts rows - the opposite way round to row totals.

questions.q: Ask the user for twelve whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a grid of four rows of three. Add up each column in turn. Add up the whole grid as well. Display [the total of each column], one on each line. Then display [the total of the whole grid] on the last line.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The total of column 0 is printed first.
Four lines of output in all.
questions.starter: # A total for each column, then one for everything

tests.why: Three column totals then the grand total. Getting 6, 15, 24, 33 and 78 means the rows were totalled instead.
Only column 0 has anything in it, and the other two still print a total of 0 rather than being skipped.
Here the last column holds everything, so a loop that stops one column short would print the wrong grand total too.

questions.fb: The column totals are worked out one at a time and the grand total grows outside that loop, so it is never reset.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for one more whole number. Store the nine in a grid of three rows of three. Count how many values in the grid are equal to or greater than that last number. Display [the count] and nothing else.

teach.say: Two loops over range(len(...)) visit every cell of a grid in turn, row by row, and a counter outside them both keeps the answer.

brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
The tenth number is not part of the grid.
A value exactly equal to it does count.
One line of output.
questions.starter: # Count the values that reach the number given

tests.why: Five of the nine values reach 5, counted across the whole grid rather than along one row.
Nothing reaches 10, so the counter stays at 0 and that 0 still has to be printed.
Every value reaches 1, so all nine count. A 3 here means only one row was visited.
Only the 9 itself reaches 9, so a value exactly equal counts and > was not what was wanted.

questions.fb: Two loops visit every cell and one counter outside them both keeps the answer, which is the shape of any count over a grid.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine words, one on each line. Then ask for a word to look for. Store the nine words in a grid of three rows of three. Find where that word is in the grid. Display [the row] and [the column] on one line, with a single space between them. Display not in the grid instead when the word is not there.
brief: The first three words typed fill row 0.
Rows and columns count from 0.
The word appears at most once in the grid.
Print exactly: not in the grid
questions.starter: # Search the grid for the word and say where it is

tests.why: Omar is in row 0, column 1. The row comes first and the column second, so printing 1 0 means the two came out the wrong way round.
Nia is in the top left, which is row 0 column 0. Printing 1 1 means rows and columns were counted from 1.
The middle cell is the one place where the row and the column match, so this test cannot tell the two apart on its own.
Yves is the very last cell, so a search that stops before the end of the last row never finds it.
A word that is nowhere in the grid prints that one line and nothing else, so the row and column are printed only once the word has been found.

questions.fb: Two loops to search every cell, and a remembered row and column that start at something impossible like -1 so you can tell afterwards whether anything was found.

questions.q: Ask the user for nine whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a whole number to look for. Store the nine in a grid of three rows of three. Find where that number is in the grid. Display not in the grid when the number is not there. Otherwise display [the row] and [the column] on one line, with a single space between them. Then add up the row the number is in. Then display [that total] on the next line.
brief: The first three numbers typed fill row 0.
Rows and columns count from 0.
The number appears at most once in the grid.
Print exactly: not in the grid
questions.starter: # Find the number, then total the row it is in

tests.why: The 1 sits in row 1, column 2, and row 1 is 7, 8, 1 which comes to 16.
The 4 is in the top left, row 0 column 0, and row 0 comes to 15. Printing 1 1 means the counting started at 1.
The 5 is the very last cell, so a search that stops before the end of the last row never finds it.
The 9 is in row 0, column 1, and the row total is the same as for the 4, because they share a row.
A number that is nowhere in the grid prints that one line and nothing else, so neither the position nor the total is printed.

questions.fb: A search over the grid and a total over one row are two separate jobs, and the second only runs once the first has found something.
